title: The crooked raffle

A host who sees it reports either "even" or "multiple of three", choosing uniformly among true reports and saying "neither" when necessary. answer:
Let \(E=\{\text{even}\}\), \(M=\{\text{multiple of 3}\}\). Among tickets \(1,\dots,60\):

- \(20\) are even but not multiples of \(3\),
- \(10\) are multiples of \(6\) (both even and multiple of \(3\)),
- \(10\) are odd multiples of \(3\),
- \(20\) are neither.

### Random true report
If a number is a multiple of \(6\), the host says “even” with probability \(1/2\).

Probability the host says “even”:
\[
P(\text{says even})
=\frac{20}{60}\cdot 1+\frac{10}{60}\cdot\frac12
=\frac{20+5}{60}
=\frac{25}{60}.
\]

Probability of both “multiple of 3” and “says even”:
\[
P(M\cap \text{says even})
=\frac{10}{60}\cdot\frac12
=\frac{5}{60}.
\]

Thus
\[
P(M\mid \text{says even})
=\frac{5/60}{25/60}
=\frac{5}{25}
=\boxed{\frac15}.
\]

### Host who always prioritizes “even”
Now any multiple of \(6\) is reported as “even,” not randomly split. So

\[
P(\text{says even})=\frac{20+10}{60}=\frac{30}{60},
\]
and among those, the multiple-of-\(3\) cases are the \(10\) multiples of \(6\). Hence
\[
P(M\mid \text{says even})
=\frac{10}{30}
=\boxed{\frac13}.
\]

So the answers are:

\[
\boxed{\frac15 \text{ for the random-report host,} \qquad \frac13 \text{ for the even-priority host.}}
\]

The reporting rule matters because it changes the selection bias among tickets that are both even and multiples of \(3\).
